data.title: JD Vance is right about stay-at-home parents — but his solution is all wrong
data.description:
Should the federal government pay parents to stay at home so they can better raise their children?

The Trump administration thinks so, and is working on plans to allow a stay-at-home spouse to collect as much as $9,000 per child each year, depending on their economic circumstances, from funds potentially available from the Health and Human Services Department. 

The driver of the program appears to be Vice President Vance, who has long championed more traditional family values where parents and “young children are clearly happier and healthier when they spend the day at home with a parent.” 

Vance is right that parents should have more opportunities to spend time with their young children. But instead of paying people not to work, why not give businesses stronger incentives to make it easier for working parents to stay home when they need to? 

Sorry if I sound so cynical, but like so many government programs, this one will almost certainly be abused.

Federal programs have had a long history of fraud, stretching from welfare, Medicare, housing and farming subsidy overpayments to the awards of food stamps, school lunches, unemployment and, most recently, COVID payments to people who did not qualify or simply swindled the government. Do we have any doubt that this handout will suffer the same consequences?

And who’s going to enforce this new program? The federal government, whose workforce has shrunk 10 percent since President Trump took office? And who will be eligible? Mothers? Fathers? Aunts? Uncles?

Good luck figuring that out — and then stopping the payments once they have started.

The $12 billion fund that Vance is targeting would mostly be distributed to states, which would then provide the funding for dependent care facilities, providers and assistance. I’m sure that’s not being abused either, right? We’ve already learned, thanks to the investigative work of some independent journalists like Nick Shirley, that most local governments not only have insufficient resources to distribute, monitor and enforce these programs but that some politicians in certain states — hello, Minnesota and California — may have, allegedly, turned a blind eye to funds being distributed to communities that could provide them with votes.    

It’s interesting that the Trump administration, a vocal backer of free markets, would put forth a program that is so much the antithesis of capitalism. At a time when many employers complain they can’t find enough workers, should taxpayers be paying some workers to leave the labor force?

If you choose to have kids, you have to make hard choices. Do both Mom and Dad have to work? If they want to afford private schools, summer camps, eating out, Netflix, Disney vacations or car leases, then sure. Good for them. We live in a great country with a high standard of living. But do the taxpayers have to pay for these choices?

Our political leaders need to make choices, too. Who doesn’t like to get paid to stay at home with our kids? But aren’t there other, more pressing priorities for our taxpayer funds? Paying down the deficit? Providing more for the military? Saving Social Security and Medicare? Reducing health care costs?  Building better roads? Better schools?

Why not take the funds that the vice president wants to spend on his stay-at-home program and put it toward those pressing needs? As much as we like to think it does, our government does not have a bottomless pit of money. I’m not sure I’d put this at the top of my list of priorities.

What’s more, we already have a number of government-funded tax benefits to encourage child care.

There is a generous individual and family tax credit, which was just expanded in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Employers get credits for providing or referring employees to day care facilities, as well as deductions for providing flexible spending accounts that can be used for dependent care.

There are tax savings for putting money into 529 plans and then using those funds for home-schooling. There is a tax credit for employers to pay people who take family leave, which was just made permanent. Many states require employers to provide paid leave for their employees. The federal government requires employers with more than 50 workers to provide unpaid leave (and hold their jobs for when employees return).

But this isn’t Vance’s priority or passion. His priority is that parents stay at home with their kids and not defer the responsibility to a child care provider. Fair enough. So instead of giving handouts for people to stay at home, wouldn’t a better approach be to expand incentives for employers?

Tax credits and deductions to pay for dependent care are fine, but I agree with Vance that there’s no better care than what a parent — at least, most parents — can provide. To that end, it would be more beneficial to explore enhanced credits for employer-funded paid parental and family leave, incentives for flexible or reduced schedules after childbirth, credits for employer-supported child care, and incentives for remote/hybrid arrangements where the job permits them.

Don’t pay parents not to work. Give employers a reason to make it easier for parents to work and raise their children at the same time. 

That way people still have incentives to work and employers have the incentive to attract and retain talent. Flexibility, whether it’s working from home or expanded paid-time-off programs, is a top benefit request for most employees.   

Vance isn’t wrong that young children benefit from spending more time with their parents. The question is who should pay for it and how. Instead of creating another government benefit that rewards people for leaving the workforce, we should give employers stronger incentives to provide the flexibility that lets parents remain in it.

Gene Marks is founder of the Marks Group, a small business consulting firm.

data.title: Bret Baier presses Paxton on Trump $5K dividend payment support
data.description:
Fox News host Bret Baier questioned Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate nominee Ken Paxton (R) on Thursday over his support for President Trump’s new controversial “Trump dividend” proposal.

At the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas this week, the president floated the idea of disbursing $5,000 checks to every adult American if Republicans maintain their majority in both chambers of Congress this fall. 

The idea has been met with pushback from Democrats and some conservatives, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) warning it could lead to “more debt and more inflation,” while left-leaning critics accuse the president of attempting to bribe the voters.

Paxton told Baier he applauded when the president introduced the idea on Wednesday evening. 

“I clapped because, look, the government takes too much of our money, people are hurting,” he said. “This is a way to help people with higher gas prices, higher energy costs and higher food prices.”

Baier pushed back, noting that the Texas attorney general advertises himself as a “strong fiscal conservative” who is committed to bringing down the national debt and counteracting rising inflation rates. 

“Arguably, the critics of this move would say, one, it increases the deficit and debt. Two, it would really spike inflation,” the Fox News host said. 

Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, has been a strong proponent of the president and his administration’s policies during his time in office and in his bid to replace Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas). The Republican is up against state Rep. James Talarico (D) in a tightly contested election this November. 

“I want to stop the spending, but I want to start returning more of what you earn to the taxpayer so that they can afford to live,” Paxton said. “Right now, the government is taking too high of a percentage for most of my constituents, and certainly, most of the country.”

Several GOP fiscal hawks have openly criticized the proposal, with former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) slamming it as a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

Republican Rep. Chip Roy (Texas) questioned how the U.S. government would pay for these disbursements. 

“Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms,” Roy wrote Thursday on social platform X. 

The president has not clarified where this money would come from. In response to a query from The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle did not provide additional details about how the proposal would work. 

“President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats’ record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage,” Ingle said in a statement. “With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results.”

data.title: Carney: Latest Trump trade moves 'relatively modest'
data.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday President Trump’s latest round of tariffs is “relatively modest” compared to the United States’ past moves. 

When talking with reporters at a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alberta, Carney was asked if Canada was going to retaliate to added U.S. tariffs.

Carney said that this government was analyzing the “significant” impact “for individual companies and in individual sectors.”

“I would also recognize that in the context of other things that the U.S. administration has done – other measures the U.S. administration has done – that these are relatively modest measures,” the prime minister said. 

The White House announced Tuesday that it would ban the import of some dairy products, motorcycles and most alcoholic beverages from Canada starting Sept. 29. This followed moves by President Trump threatening to ban Canadian private jet maker Bombardier from selling its products in U.S. markets. 

Trump’s threat is already garnering backlash from GOP lawmakers, including Kansas Sens. Jerry Moran (R) and Roger Marshall (R), who pointed out that the company was a major employer in the Sunflower State.

Carney confirmed that the two-day cabinet retreat would be discussing the ongoing trade war’s impact and “have a chance to draw that out in more detail” following the country’s own tariffs going into effect this week.

He also said that Canada “are always ready to sit down” because “there is a mutually beneficial deal possible that respects our sovereignty and is in the interests of both countries.”

“We take into context that the biggest impact we can have here in Canada is to focus on what we can control, building at home, diversifying abroad, and delivering for Canadians,” Carney said. “I engage with the president of the United States on a wide range of issues and issues of geopolitical defense and security.”

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on $27.6 billion of American products went into effect Tuesday. The 15, 25 and 50 percent tariffs affected close to 6 percent of what the U.S. exported to Canada last year.

data.title: US must adopt the Finland model for producing warships
data.description:
Last month, President Trump issued a memorandum on “Rebuilding the United States Navy and America’s Shipbuilding Industrial Base.” It called for the Navy to adopt what it terms the “Finland Model” for warship construction.

The memo states that “this Finland Model” is to be used to produce surface ships for anti-submarine warfare, “consolidated cargo replenishment” tankers, and “roll-on, roll-off vessels.”

The arrangement, whose official designation is the Icebreaker Collaboration Agreement or ICEPact, is a three way agreement among the U.S., Canada and Finland to modernize the American and Canadian icebreaker fleets. The deal will enable the Coast Guard to acquire four icebreakers from Finland, with seven more to be built in American shipyards. As a result, the Coast Guard will be able to replace its aging icebreaker fleet quickly.

Construction on the first of the Coast Guard Arctic Security Cutters began in June at the Sata Shipbuilding yard in Finland. Delivery of the icebreaker is on schedule and according to local observers in Helsinki, the program also is on budget.

Two months earlier, the Bollinger shipyard in Houma, La. welded together the first steel sheets of an Arctic Security Cutter design for an icebreaker being built in parallel with a second Finnish shipbuilder, Rauma Marine Constructions.

Trump’s memorandum incorporates several aspects of the Finland model. It requires that foreign shipbuilders building U.S. military craft establish a robust presence within the U.S., building shipyards and hiring U.S. workers even as they build ships abroad. They must also license their “proprietary shipbuilding techniques and technologies” to U.S. shipyards and create U.S. supply chains “for construction and maintenance of all ships” they build in the U.S.

The Finland model offers a blueprint that would enable the US Navy to begin to address its urgent need to increase its force levels and create lasting naval shipbuilding capacity. It holds out the prospects for additional serial warship production, incorporating advanced propulsion and a resilient supplier base.

The Finland model will also yield a capable workforce. Like shipbuilding more generally, Arctic shipbuilding depends on welders, pipefitters, electricians, naval architects, marine engineers, propulsion specialists, and shipyard supervisors. The workforce that emerges from the ICEPact Program would be a welcome addition to the current workforce supporting naval construction.

In order to implement Trump’s plan, foreign shipyards would have to receive some sort of waiver from the State Department’s International Traffic in Arms Regulations which constrain the export of technical data that would be needed to construct the ships to the Navy’s specifications. In addition, ships built in foreign yards would have to allow for both stringent Navy redundancy and survivability standards and for the insertion of the Navy’s combat systems once they are towed to American yards.

It is not impossible to find ways to accommodate whatever technical and other restrictions that might be imposed on foreign shipbuilders. On the other hand, it is far more difficult to win Congressional approval for employing the Finland model for construction of surface combatants.

The administration’s plan has already run into heavy congressional opposition. Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), home to the Bath Iron Works shipyard, has successfully inserted an amendment to the pending fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act that specifies that no fiscal 2027 funds can be obligated for procurement of a battle force ship to be built outside the U.S. His express purpose is to “block [the] Pentagon from sending U.S. shipbuilding jobs overseas.” Not surprisingly, Golden has the support of representatives from other shipbuilding states.

Were the shipyards suffering from bare order books, Golden and those who support his amendment would have a case for restricting overseas shipbuilding for the Navy. But that is not true at all. As the Government Accountability Office’s director of contracting and national security acquisitions testified before two Congressional subcommittees in April, the shipyards are not even meeting construction schedules for ships already under contract. A shortage of backlogs is not the problem.

With China projected to have a battle force of 435 ships by 2030, as compared to the U.S. Navy’s goal of reaching 381 ships more than a decade later, it is imperative that members of Congress, even those who hail from states with shipyards, reconsider their opposition to applying the Finland model to Navy warships.

That model would not only provide the Navy with more ships more quickly, but it would actually accomplish what those members are seeking: more jobs at home for an expanded and well-trained American workforce.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Collins: Trump's proposed $5K dividend 'extraordinarily costly'
data.description:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) says that President Trump’s proposal to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win the midterm election “would be extraordinarily costly” and questioned providing it to everyone regardless of financial need.

“From the few details we have, it seems that the proposed $5,000 dividend would not have an income cap and would be extraordinarily costly,” Collins said in a statement.

“Tax and spending decisions should be made based on the needs of the American people and the state of the economy, they should not appear to be tied to election results,” she said.

Collins has emerged as one of the highest-profile GOP critics of the proposal, which would cost more than $1 trillion and add to the nation’s $40 trillion debt unless Congress finds a way to offset it.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) defended the idea during an interview with Fox News as a proposal to put more money into the pockets of Americans.

But Thune hesitated on whether the GOP-controlled Senate would take up the proposal on the floor and attempt to pass it.

“Well, that’s a good question,” he said. “We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it.”

Fiscal conservatives have panned the idea.

Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.), a past chair of the House Freedom Caucus, dismissed the proposal as a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

data.title: Former presidents reflect on 9/11: 'We can't erase the nightmare'
data.description:
Former American presidents on Friday reflected on the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks as the U.S. marks the 25th anniversary of the tragic day. 

“We can’t erase the nightmare that so many have lived through and are still living with today, but we can support the people who have given and lost so much by treating one another with respect, in person and online, and recognizing that what we have in common is far more important than what divides us,” former President Clinton wrote in a statement. 

“As 9/11 moves further from lived experience into history, may we always take this solemn anniversary to come together and keep alive the memories of all who were lost,” he continued. “We owe that to them, to their loved ones, to each other, and to future generations.”

All living former heads of state and Vice President JD Vance are attending a Friday ceremony at Ground Zero in New York City. President Trump is participating in a memorial at the Pentagon, joined by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, first lady Melania Trump and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice.

A total of 2,977 people died during these attacks on the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon in Arlington, Va., and at the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93 in Pennsylvania. 

In a statement released Friday, former President Obama commemorated the lives lost during these attacks and commended the rescue workers who responded that day. 

“Today Michelle and I are remembering those we lost that day, and those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the wars that followed,” Obama wrote.

“We pray for their families,” he continued. “And we hope Americans everywhere remember the true lesson of 9/11: that we can survive even our darkest days as long as we move forward as one nation and one people.”

Former President George W. Bush, who was serving as president during the attacks, reflected on his administration’s response to the attacks during a Wednesday conversation with Rice at his presidential library in Dallas.

Bush recalled the moment his White House chief of staff, Andrew Card, informed him during an event with schoolchildren that the second World Trade Center tower had been struck. 

“I didn’t have much time to process that, but it was pretty clear to me that if we were under attack, that my job was to defend the child that was reading to me and her family and her country,” he said. “And so, it was a moment of clarity.”

The former commander in chief added, “I knew we had to gather evidence, and we had to gather the facts, but I assumed we were under attack.”

data.title: Joe DiGenova resigns from DOJ position investigating Trump foes
data.description:
Joe DiGenova, a Trump ally tapped to lead a sprawling investigation into many of the president’s perceived enemies, resigned from the post late Thursday, indicating concerns over the strength of the case.

The so-called grand conspiracy investigation was led out of a U.S. attorney office in Florida where prosecutors issued dozens of subpoenas in a sweeping probe into the 2016 election and the cases into President Trump. 

“I did in fact resign,” diGenova told The Associated Press, calling it an “honor and a privilege” to serve Trump and the Justice Department.

But in a later interview with The New York Post, diGenova suggested there were larger issues with the investigation.

“If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem,” he told the outlet.

DiGenova later expanded on those comments to The Associated Press, saying “There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”

The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment. ABC News first reported his resignation.

The probe has yet to lead to any charges.

Throughout the course of the investigation, prosecutors have been focused on former CIA Director John Brennan, who in July sued to prompt preservation of all files related to a potential case.

Prosecutors have also sought information from those who worked on the Mar-a-Lago documents case into Trump.

data.title: Why Trump is leaning into his role as 'builder-in-chief'
data.description:
You’d think that a self-described genius like Donald Trump would have more sense than to post an AI-generated image on social media declaring “Mission Accomplished” in Iran.

For one thing, the mission is not accomplished. Iran still has the capacity to build a nuclear bomb, and missiles are still flying over the Strait of Hormuz.

So how exactly is the mission accomplished?

And you’d think the president might have learned something from another president — George W. Bush, who stood in front of a giant “Mission Accomplished” banner aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln while the war in Iraq wasn’t even close to being over.

Mission accomplished became a symbol of failure — and ammunition for the war’s critics.

But there’s something else intriguing about all of this.

With no end in sight to the conflict with Iran, Donald Trump seems eager to change the subject. And what would he rather talk about if not missiles or nuclear enrichment or the Strait of Hormuz?

He’d rather talk about architecture than a war he calls “small potatoes.”

More specifically, he’d rather talk about how he’s changing the face of the White House — and a good part of Washington along with it.

He loves talking about his grand, gold-laced ballroom. Then there’s the magnificent 250-foot triumphal arch, sometimes called the Arch de Trump. And there’s the Reflecting Pool he’s trying to make look — if not exactly beautiful — at least halfway decent.

As for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, he’s still trying to rename it, with his name getting top billing. And there’s the facelift he wants to give a public golf course near the National Mall.

There’s more.

The president doesn’t like the looks of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, so he’s pushing to have the granite exterior of the historic structure painted white. And he’d like to build a garden honoring 250 notable Americans, complete with life-size statues, reflecting pools, plazas and an amphitheater.

As The New York Times put it, “As the United States appears mired in another intractable conflict in the Middle East, Mr. Trump has basked in the momentum he has on the half-dozen makeover projects he has set in motion throughout the capital.”

The Times also reports that “He is at his most animated, aides and visitors to the White House say, when he is showing off the designs for the ballroom, boasting about the size of the columns and their designs.”

“Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, no other president has done more to beautify our nation’s interior than President Trump,” a White House spokesman said.

And maybe “Builder-in-Chief” tells us more than the spokesman intended.

Because building is a lot easier to talk about than Iran.

A ballroom has blueprints. An arch has dimensions. A building can be painted white. And when somebody asks how the project is going, the president can point to something and say: Look what I built.

A war is different.

Wars don’t always follow the plans. The other side gets a vote. Enemies don’t necessarily cooperate with your timetable. And when you declare “Mission Accomplished,” inconvenient things can keep happening — missiles can still fly, ships can still come under attack, and the mission can stubbornly refuse to be accomplished.

Which may explain why Donald Trump seems so much more comfortable talking about columns and ballrooms than about how and when the war with Iran is actually going to end.

“I’m a really good builder,” Trump told reporters earlier this year. “The thing I do best in life is build.”

Maybe he’s right.

And given the choice between explaining a war he hasn’t figured out how to end and showing reporters a ballroom he knows exactly how he wants to finish, is there really any mystery about which Donald Trump would rather talk about?

One last thing: When was the last time you heard the president refer to his grand ballroom or the “Arch de Trump” as “small potatoes”?

How about never.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page.

data.title: Live updates: Trump, Vance, past presidents pause to remember Sept. 11
data.description:
President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are attending a remembrance at the Pentagon, while Vice President Vance has joined past presidents and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani at Ground Zero on Friday morning, as America pauses to honor the victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Twenty-five years after four jets took down the World Trade Center, crashed into the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania, the Trump administration is stepping gingerly into a loosening of tight airport security measures implemented in the aftermath.

Mamdani, a Muslim, has faced criticism for plans to attend the ceremony at Ground Zero. Some 9/11 families, along with former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, have cited past critical remarks from Mamdani’s political allies.

The solemn day follows two days of cheerleading in Dallas for the Trump administration and Republican midterm candidates. Vance closed the convention amid growing chatter about his 2028 prospects. His Thursday night keynote offered the vice president a chance to charm the base that will be critical if he decides to run to succeed Trump in the next election.

The president will return to the White House for signing time before departing later Friday for Dublin, Ireland. He’ll spend the weekend at his golf resort for the Irish Open.

data.title: El-Sayed on GOP convention attendee's call for him to be shot: 'Call it out for what it is'
data.description:
Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Thursday that he hoped that Republicans “call it out for what it is” when discussing shouts from a GOP Midterm convention attendee that called for he and other Democratic lawmakers to be shot.

In an interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, El-Sayed was asked about a clip that showed a member of the audience shouting, “He should be shot!” while Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) listed Democrats during his Thursday remarks – including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico.

It is unclear if Cruz could hear the audience member from the stage as he did not acknowledge the shouts. The incident came on the one-year anniversary of conservative political commentator Charlie Kirk’s assassination, an occasion marked at the GOP convention including by Cruz during his speech Thursday.

“Look, I’m a dad with two daughters, and I hope those daughters get to grow up and live with their dad. This is what has become norm in our politics, I mean, literally calls to violence and the inability for anybody to actually call it out,” El-Sayed told Collins. 

“We can learn to disagree agreeably, and when you hear that kind of call to violence, it should be shuddering to all of us. We have a responsibility to lower the temperature, to release that this is not a bloodsport, where you’re just trying to bash the other guy,” he said.

“And so I hope that everybody who heard that is going to call it out for what it is: a call to violence that ought to be condemned across the board,” he continued.

El-Sayed concluded that he hoped, “we can actually turn our politics back into a conversation about what really matters” which is “the ability to live a dignified life, get the things that you need and deserve in your life, and recognize that our democracy.”

He is currently leading his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) by 3 points in a Wednesday CNN poll, with 47 percent support to the GOP candidate’s 44 percent. 

The race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) has become a battleground election with both parties hoping to take the Senate majority with wins in Michigan.

Cruz’s office did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.
